name.description:
The name is the label under which this test will be recorded in the PerfMetric database. It usually comes from
the type and method name, for example "Type.fromString".

oneRun.description:
The action to be measured in a single run of the test.

A sample lambda should look like this:

    ```
    (lambdaIterations) -> {
        for (int i = 0; i < lambdaIterations; i++) {
            Dog.make()
        }
    }
    ```

Note `lambdaIterations` is a parameter that will be used by the framework during measuring. With this parameter, the
framework can dynamically compute an ideal number of iterations to execute the action so that the lambda runs for
_at least_ 5 seconds (configurable, see {@link MicrobenchSpec#runTime}) to get a stable result. The framework will
also scale the result as if the action runs `numIterations` time, which is the goal of the measurement. The minimum
running time allows both just-in-time code generation and garbage collection to stabilize. Normally, the first run
will be the longest and successive runs will be several times faster. If the lambda returns an object, its size is
measured and recorded as "retained memory" (see {@link MicrobenchResult#retainedMem}).

Note that if the lambda returns a {@link MicrobenchResult} object, the measurement should be done by the lambda
itself and the test will pick up the returned MicrobenchResult object as the test result.

title:
A single performance-centric unit test. An instance can be created and executed explicitly or one of the convenience
methods can be used set up a set of related tests to be executed together for comparison purposes.

These are called "micro benchmarks" because they are focused unit tests. For larger-scale distributed PSR testing,
see {@link MaximGun}.

When these tests are run, summary output is printed and the results are logged in the {@link PerfMetric} database.
The details of this behavior can be configured using the {@link MicrobenchSpec}. The results are collected into a
{@link MicrobenchResultSet}.

The code being tested is always wrapped in a lambda, which is passed to #test, #compare, #measureKpi, etc.
This is what the microbench framework "sees" and is the smallest amount of code execution that is measured.
Each time tested this lambda will be executed, making a "run".

Initially, {@link MicrobenchSpec#numRuns} and {@link MicrobenchSpec#runTime runTime} will be used, but over time
runs will only be executed until the historical average is beaten. See {@link MicrobenchSpec#resultsToBeat}.

Note that if the code being tested executes so fast that the measurement would swamp the actual execution time,
looping must be done inside the lambda itself. A rule of thumb is that the lambda should take a second or more, not
only for measurement overhead, but also so that Java and JavaScript code is fully compiled into machine code.

@see MicrobenchResultSet
name: Microbench
